Filadelfia is located in the Chaco and is closely connected with the history of Mennonite settlements. From town, visitors set out to explore lagoons, natural areas and neighboring communities. A stop here offers time to experience everyday life in the region.

The Jakob Unger Museum explores the history of the colonies, including Filadelfia, Loma Plata, Neuland and Menno. The story of these settlers helps explain how roads, farms and communities developed in the dry Chaco environment. Filadelfia adds a cultural perspective to nature excursions, illuminating both the settlement history and present-day life of the region.

Filandia retains its colonial buildings and compact streets, making it easy to explore on foot. Colorful façades and local cafés invite visitors to linger between nature excursions in the Coffee Region. One of the town's prominent landmarks, the Quindío viewpoint, opens up views of the surrounding landscape.

The town is also a place to discover local cuisine. Visitors sample regional drinks and desserts in restaurants and cafés before continuing their walk through the streets. Filandia is part of the same travel region as Salento and the Cocora Valley, so a day in town complements a visit to the palm forest.

The Fish Islands lie near Prospect Point, off the coast of Graham Land. The group comprises several small islands and rocks. Cold waters, exposed rocky shores and floating ice shape the scenery.

The islands were charted by members of the British Graham Land Expedition in 1935. Expedition cruises visit to observe Adélie penguins and Antarctic shags. Wildlife is watched from accessible stretches of shore or from boats, while maintaining a respectful distance from the animals.

Flamenco Island lies beside Panama City and is connected with Pacific Ocean sailing routes. Its port serves as a boarding point for ships and yachts. The piers and marinas provide a view of the capital's maritime side after exploring its city neighborhoods.

Flamenco connects with the Amador Causeway and coastal views of the Gulf of Panama. From here, travelers depart for island destinations and continue their yacht journeys. A stop on the island brings together the city's waterfront and open water, as the capital gradually gives way to a sea voyage.

Flamingo lies on Costa Rica's northwestern Pacific coast. The area is known for sea fishing excursions: some routes head into deep ocean waters, while others stay closer to the Catalina and Brummel islands. The waters differ in depth and in the fish species that attract anglers.

Sailfish, marlin, mahi-mahi and tuna inhabit the open ocean. Fishing around the islands focuses on wahoo, mackerel and roosterfish. Flamingo appeals to travelers who want fishing to be a dedicated part of their Costa Rica itinerary and who plan to spend several days beside the Pacific.
